Yes, a bounded analytic function can have an unbounded derivative.

**Proof.**

We work on the open unit disk $\mathbb{D} = \{z \in \mathbb{C} : |z|<1\}$.

Define $f(z) = (1-z)^{1/2}$, using the principal branch of the square root. This is well-defined and analytic on $\mathbb{D}$: for $z \in \mathbb{D}$, the value $1-z$ lies in the disk $\{w : |w-1|<1\}$, which is contained in the open right half-plane $\{w : \operatorname{Re} w > 0\}$. In particular $1-z$ never touches the non-positive real axis (the branch cut of the principal square root), so $\log(1-z)$ is analytic on $\mathbb{D}$, and $f(z) = \exp\!\big(\tfrac{1}{2}\log(1-z)\big)$ is analytic on $\mathbb{D}$.

**$f$ is bounded.** For $z \in \mathbb{D}$,
$$|f(z)| = |1-z|^{1/2} \le (|1|+|z|)^{1/2} < 2^{1/2},$$
so $f$ is bounded on $\mathbb{D}$.

**$f'$ is unbounded.** Differentiating,
$$f'(z) = -\tfrac{1}{2}(1-z)^{-1/2}.$$
Consider the sequence $z_n = 1 - \tfrac{1}{n}$ for $n \ge 2$. Then $z_n \in \mathbb{D}$ (since $|z_n| = 1 - \tfrac{1}{n} < 1$), and
$$|f'(z_n)| = \tfrac{1}{2}\,|1-z_n|^{-1/2} = \tfrac{1}{2}\left(\tfrac{1}{n}\right)^{-1/2} = \tfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{n} \xrightarrow{n\to\infty} \infty.$$
Hence $f'$ is unbounded on $\mathbb{D}$.

We have exhibited a function that is analytic and bounded on a domain, yet whose derivative is unbounded there. Therefore the answer is **yes**.
